Following the PCA analysis, which suggested that some clinically relevant variables were not strongly represented by the main principal components, this analysis aimed to investigate the relationship between lifestyle factors, preexisting illnesses and mortality. How are lifestyle factors and pre-existing illnesses, individually and in combination, associated with mortality among patients?

Loading library

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(broom)
```

Load clean data

```{r}
clean_data <- read_tsv(file = "../data/03_dat_aug.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r}
view(clean_data)
```

Preparing lifestyle and illness variables (death, smoking, alcohol consumption, physical activity, coronary hear disease, congestive heart failure, stroke, diabetes)

```{r}
lifestyle_data <- clean_data |> 
  select(death, smoker, alcoh, physact,
         chf, chd, diabetes) |> 
  mutate(
    smoker = case_when(
      smoker == "never" ~ "Never smoked",
      smoker == "current" | smoker == "former" ~ "Smoked"
    ),
    alcoh = if_else(
      alcoh > 0,
      "Consumed alcohol",
      "Did not consume alcohol"
    ),
    physact = if_else(
      physact > 0,
      "Physically active",
      "Physically inactive"
    ),
    chf = if_else(chf == 1, "Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)", "No CHF"),
    diabetes = if_else(diabetes == 1,
                       "Diabetes", "No diabetes"),
    chd = if_else(chd > 0, "Coronary heart disease (CHD)", "No CHD")
  )

view(lifestyle_data)
```

Checking if we have na values in lifestyle data

```{r}

colSums(is.na(lifestyle_data))
```

Calculating mortality percentage

```{r}
mortality_summary <- lifestyle_data |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -death,
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "category"
  ) |> 
  group_by(variable, category) |> 
  summarise(
    total_patients = n(),
    number_deaths = sum(death == 1),
    percentage_death = number_deaths / total_patients * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

view(mortality_summary)
```

Visualizing all characteristics by mortality percentage

```{r}
plot <- mortality_summary |>
  mutate(
    characteristic = paste(category)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = reorder(category, percentage_death),
    y = percentage_death
  )) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = category == "Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)" | category == "Diabetes"),
         width = 0.6) +
scale_fill_manual(
  values = c("TRUE" = "firebrick", "FALSE" = "steelblue"),
  guide = "none"
) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(
      round(percentage_death, 1), "%"
    )),
    hjust = -0.2,
    size = 4
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Characteristics by mortality",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Mortality (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot

ggsave(
  "../results/07_analysis_3/characteristics_plot.png",
  plot,
  width = 14,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)
```

Patients with CHF and diabetes showed high observed mortality percentages of 40% and 31.8%, respectively. Although smoking alone was not previously found to be statistically significantly associated with mortality, investigating lifestyle characteristics alongside pre-existing illnesses may reveal additional mortality patterns. From a biological perspective, smoking and physical inactivity may contribute to cardiovascular complications and impaired metabolic regulation. However, small patient groups and potential confounding factors, such as age and sex, limit the interpretation of these findings.

Is the combination of pre-existing illnesses and lifestyle factors (smoking and diabetes) is associated with higher mortality?

Selecting only patients with CHF and dividing it into four lifestyle groups

```{r}
chf_summary <- lifestyle_data |>
  filter(chf == "Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)") |>
  group_by(smoker, physact) |>
  summarise(
    total_patients = n(),
    number_deaths = sum(death == 1),
    number_alive = sum(death == 0),
    percentage_death = number_deaths / total_patients * 100,
    .groups = "drop"

chf_summary
```

```{r}
chf_test <- lifestyle_data |>
  filter(chf == "Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)") |>
  unite(profile, smoker, physact, sep = " + ")

fisher.test(table(chf_test$profile, chf_test$death))
```

Although patients with CHF had the highest overall mortality percentage (40%), differences in mortality across smoking and physical activity profiles were not statistically significant. However, the relatively small number of patients with CHF may limit the ability to detect an association.

```{r}
diabetes_test <- lifestyle_data |>
  filter(diabetes == "Diabetes") |>
  unite(profile, smoker, physact, sep = " + ")

fisher.test(table(diabetes_test$profile, diabetes_test$death))
```

The analysis demonstrated that patients with CHF and diabetes had high mortality percentages of 40% and 31.8%, respectively. Fisher's exact test revealed a statistically significant association between combined smoking and physical activity profiles and mortality among patients with diabetes (p = 0.01782), whereas no significant association was found among patients with CHF (p = 0.7729). These findings highlight the importance of investigating lifestyle factors alongside pre-existing illnesses to better understand mortality patterns. However, small patient groups and potential confounding factors limit the interpretation of these results, and no causal relationship can be established.

After discussing with AI he suggested using Fishers test as it is better for small sample numbers. Are we leaving both statistical tests?

The statistically significant result suggests that lifestyle characteristics, specifically combinations of smoking history and physical activity, are associated with mortality among patients with diabetes. This is biologically plausible because smoking and physical inactivity can contribute to cardiovascular complications and impaired glucose regulation.

Statistical tests for the combinations, using logistic regression: to test whether smoking exposure and CHF/ smoking exposure and diabetes show a statistically significant interaction or joint effect on death.

Smoking + CHF combinations

```{r}
chf_four_group_data <- lifestyle_data |>
  filter(chf == "Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)") |>
  drop_na(smoker, physact, death) |>
  mutate(
    profile = paste(smoker, physact, sep = " + ") |>
      factor(levels = c(
        "Never smoked + Physically active",
        "Smoked + Physically active",
        "Never smoked + Physically inactive",
        "Smoked + Physically inactive"
      ))
  )

chf_four_group_model <- glm(
  formula = death ~ profile,
  data = chf_four_group_data,
  family = binomial()
)

chf_four_group_results <- tidy(
  x = chf_four_group_model,
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  conf.int = TRUE
)

chf_four_group_results
```

Compared with the reference group of patients with neither smoking exposure nor CHF, having smoking exposure alone without CHF is not significantly associated with higher mortality odds. By contrast, mortality odds are significantly higher for patients with CHF alone and highest for those with both smoking exposure and CHF.

The (Intercept) row gives the baseline odds of death for the healthiest reference group (No smoking exposure + No CHF).

Smoking + diabetes combinations

```{r}
diab_four_group_data <- lifestyle_data |>
  filter(diabetes == "Diabetes") |>
  drop_na(smoker, physact, death) |>
  mutate(
    profile = paste(smoker, physact, sep = " + ") |>
      factor(levels = c(
        "Never smoked + Physically active",
        "Smoked + Physically active",
        "Never smoked + Physically inactive",
        "Smoked + Physically inactive"
      ))
  )

diab_four_group_model <- glm(
  formula = death ~ profile,
  data = diab_four_group_data,
  family = binomial()
)

diab_four_group_results <- tidy(
  x = diab_four_group_model,
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  conf.int = TRUE
)

diab_four_group_results
```

Compared with the reference group of patients with neither smoking exposure nor diabetes, neither smoking exposure alone without diabetes or diabetes alone without smoking exposure shows a statistically significant difference in mortality odds. By contrast, patients with both smoking exposure and diabetes have significantly higher mortality odds.

The (Intercept) row gives the baseline odds of death for that healthiest reference group (No smoking exposure + No diabetes).

Save data

```{r}
write_tsv(x = chf_four_group_results,
  file = "../results/07_analysis_3/smoking_chf_glm.tsv")

write_tsv(x = diab_four_group_results,
  file = "../results/07_analysis_3/smoking_diabetes_glm.tsv")
```
